passages.title: Questions 51–55
passages.body:
It must not be imagined that a walking tour, as some would have us fancy, is merely a better or worse way of seeing the country. There are many ways of seeing landscape quite as good; and none more vivid, in spite of canting dilettantes, than from a railway train. But landscape on a walking tour is quite an accessory. He who is indeed of the brotherhood does not voyage in quest of the picturesque, but of certain jolly humours — of the hope and spirit with which the march begins at morning, and the peace and spiritual repletion of the evening's rest. He cannot tell whether he puts his knapsack on, or takes it off, with more delight. The excitement of the departure puts him in key for that of the arrival. Whatever he does is not only a reward in itself, but will be further rewarded in the sequel; and so pleasure leads on to pleasure in an endless chain. It is this that so few can understand; they will either be always lounging or always at five miles an hour; they do not play off the one against the other, prepare all day for the evening, and all evening for the next day.

Now, to be properly enjoyed, a walking tour should be gone upon alone. If you go in a company, or even in pairs, it is no longer a walking tour in anything but name; it is something else and more in the nature of a picnic. A walking tour should be gone upon alone, because freedom is of the essence; because you should be able to stop and go on, and follow this way or that, as the freak takes you; and because you must have your own pace, and neither trot alongside a champion walker, nor mince in time with a girl. And then you must be open to all impressions and let your thoughts take colour from what you see. You should be as a pipe for any wind to play upon. "I cannot see the wit," says Hazlitt, "of walking and talking at the same time. When I am in the country I wish to vegetate like the country" — which is the gist of all that can be said upon the matter. There should be no cackle of voices at your elbow, to jar on the meditative silence of the morning. And so long as a man is reasoning he cannot surrender himself to that fine intoxication that comes of much motion in the open air, that begins in a sort of dazzle and sluggishness of the brain, and ends in a peace that passes comprehension.

passages.title: Questions 56–60
passages.body:
Historical analysis combines several levels of thinking and study, posing a question about the past, setting up the problem in a form intended to facilitate its solution, solving the problem, and verifying the solution or interpretation. Academic history relies on formal analysis, based on rational and systematic apprehension of relevant evidence. Yet such formal analysis can be seen as a subset of the broader category of interpretation, including responses to evidence that are impressionistic and informal rather than formal and logically structured. Indeed, the many genres of academic and popular history run the full gamut from logically systematic to impressionistic.

Historians come from a widely varying range of philosophical traditions, and the varying philosophies lead to quite different ways of posing questions and answers. The distinctions among philosophical principles sketched here help to show how it is that different analytical priorities arise on the main topics proposed for analysis; they also show how historians can rely on similar data yet come to different or conflicting conclusions. Nineteenth century philosophical outlooks remain central to the world-historical analysis: most notably the dialectics of G.W.F. Hegel and the materialism of Karl Marx. Another great nineteenth-century current of thought was positivism, elaborated by Auguste Comte and focusing on study through breaking large problems into small ones, seeking deterministic relationship within the smaller problems. Philosophies of structuralism and post modernism have developed in more recent times, rejecting the positivist separation of problems into discrete sub-problems and emphasizing interaction among aspects of a problem.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

__Consequently__, this poses a threat to agriculture and human health.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'Consequently' modifies the whole sentence and means 'as a result', so it is an adverb.
Answer: (b) Adverb.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

His __only__ answer was a grunt.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'Only' comes before the noun 'answer' and describes it, so it is an adjective.
Answer: (b) Adjective.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

__To swim__ every day is good for health.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'To' + base verb is an infinitive. A gerund would be 'Swimming'.
Answer: (b) Infinitive verb.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

I didn't tell him anything __except__ that I needed the money.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'Except' introduces the clause 'that I needed the money', so it works as a conjunction. The two web keys disagree ((c) and (d)); see review flags.
Answer: (d) Conjunction.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

She married at 18 and gave birth to her first child shortly __thereafter__.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'Thereafter' means 'after that' and modifies the verb phrase, so it is an adverb.
Answer: (d) Adverb.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

He is one of the tallest boys in __his__ class.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'His' shows possession; among the given options it is a possessive pronoun (it is also called a possessive adjective).
Answer: (a) Possessive Pronoun.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

The __mighty__ river Brahmaputra flows through the plains of Assam.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'Mighty' describes the noun 'river', so it is an adjective.
Answer: (b) Adjective.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

The money which one earns is not the money for __himself__, it is for the family and society.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'Himself' refers back to 'one', so it is a (reflexive) pronoun.
Answer: (b) Pronoun.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

The Principal said, "We should __always__ be disciplined."
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'Always' modifies the verb phrase 'be disciplined', so it is an adverb.
Answer: (b) Adverb.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Identify the part of the speech of the underlined word or phrase.

The __river__ that flows through the village is a tributary of the Cauvery.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Part of speech depends on the job a word does in the sentence.
Step 1: 'River' names a thing, so it is a noun.
Answer: (b) Noun.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: According to the passage, what is the primary purpose of a walking tour?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Main idea.
Step 1: The author says landscape is only 'an accessory' and the true walker seeks not the picturesque but 'certain jolly humours', so that 'pleasure leads on to pleasure in an endless chain'. The web keys disagree ((c) vs (a)); the passage supports (c).
Answer: (c) Longing for pleasure.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: According to the passage, a walking tour should be gone upon alone because :
questions.opt_a: It is more in the nature of a picnic.
questions.opt_b: He may put his knapsack on, or take it off, with more delight.
questions.opt_c: It will add to individual excitement.
questions.opt_d: It will provide freedom which is of the utmost importance.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the reason in the passage.
Step 1: 'A walking tour should be gone upon alone, because freedom is of the essence'.
Answer: (d) It will provide freedom which is of the utmost importance..
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: According to the passage, what can adversely affect the walking tour?
questions.opt_a: Walking and talking at the same time
questions.opt_b: Walking to rise above the everyday worries of life
questions.opt_c: Walking to experience the beauty of the surroundings
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the line in the passage.
Step 1: Quoting Hazlitt, the author says he 'cannot see the wit of walking and talking at the same time' and wants 'no cackle of voices'.
Answer: (a) Walking and talking at the same time.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: According to the passage, how should a walking tour conclude?
questions.opt_a: With the meditative peace above the real surroundings
questions.opt_b: With a peace that delights you
questions.opt_c: With the impressions of the surroundings
questions.opt_d: With the sounds of the birds around you
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the line in the passage.
Step 1: The passage says the motion in the open air 'ends in a peace that passes comprehension', so the tour ends in a delightful peace.
Answer: (b) With a peace that delights you.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: Which of the following does not amount to historical analysis?
questions.opt_a: Posing a question about the past, setting up the problem in a form intended to facilitate its solution.
questions.opt_b: Solving the problem and verifying the solution or interpretation.
questions.opt_c: Combines several levels of thinking and study to arrive at a conclusion.
questions.opt_d: Drawing from evidence to make impressionistic and informal conclusion.
questions.explanation:
Concept: A 'not' item needs the one statement the passage does not support.
Step 1: Options (a), (b) and (c) are the levels of historical analysis listed in the first sentence. Impressionistic and informal responses fall under the broader category of interpretation, not formal analysis. The web keys disagree ((d) vs (b)); the passage supports (d).
Answer: (d) d.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: 'The many genres of academic and popular history run the full gamut from logically systematic to impressionistic' means :
questions.opt_a: The range of texts varies from those based on objective analysis and those based on subjective assertions.
questions.opt_b: Historical analysis that is rarely vague to that which establishes evidence.
questions.opt_c: Historical analysis that is always vague to that which establishes no evidence.
questions.opt_d: Historical analysis that is rarely systematic to that which establishes evidence.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Inference.
Step 1: 'Full gamut' means the whole range. The writing ranges from logical, systematic (objective) to impressionistic (subjective).
Answer: (a) The range of texts varies from those based on objective analysis and those based on subjective assertions..
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question:
What, according to the author, makes historians come to conflicting conclusions?
1. They are influenced by their philosophical beliefs in asking questions on the same data.
2. They apply different interpretations on the same data.
3. They go for the primary data and evidence.
4. They are influenced by the current political developments.

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Concept: Statement-based item.
Step 1: The passage says philosophies lead to different ways of posing questions and that historians 'rely on similar data yet come to different or conflicting conclusions'. Statements 1 and 2 match.
Step 2: Nothing says they prefer primary data (3) or follow current politics (4).
Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only.

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.theme: Word for a view of determinism

questions.explanation:
Concept: Vocabulary in context.
Step 1: Determinism is the view that events and actions are caused by factors outside one's will. The passage uses 'deterministic relationship'.
Answer: (c) Deterministic relationship.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: Which one of the following relates to the post-modernist approach to History?
questions.opt_b: Post-modernist approach emphasises interaction among aspects of a problem.
questions.opt_c: Post-modernist approach rejects both; the separation of problems into sub-problems and interaction among them.
questions.opt_d: Post-modernist approach supports separation of problems and interaction among them.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Factual detail.
Step 1: Structuralism and post modernism reject 'the positivist separation of problems into discrete sub-problems' and emphasise 'interaction among aspects of a problem'.
Answer: (b) Post-modernist approach emphasises interaction among aspects of a problem..
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

This sauce has to be used ______ 23rd September.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

I'll be working on this report ______ 10:30 p.m.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

Directions: Select whichever preposition or determiner you consider the most appropriate for the blank space.

I have ______ energy left to complete the work.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:

I had ______ trouble finding the house.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

______ of these officers are very well-trained.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

I don't like going to ______ dentist.

questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:

They placed the African elephant ______ their endangered list.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

______ travel industry is changing rapidly.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

She is ______ MP from Rajasthan.

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose (d).

__Everything__ (a) __what happened__ (b) __was because of my actions.__ (c)

Answer: (b).
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose (d).

__Some people__ (a) __could write well__ (b) __while others didn't.__ (c)
questions.explanation:
Concept: Parallel clauses use the same verb form.
Step 1: 'could write well while others couldn't' keeps the modal. 'didn't' breaks the parallel. Both web keys mark (c); DP's blind answer was (d).
Answer: (c).
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose (d).

__The police are working hard__ (a) __until they are able to__ (b) __arrest the culprits.__ (c)
questions.explanation:
Concept: Purpose is shown with 'so that' or 'to'.
Step 1: 'working hard until they are able to arrest' wrongly uses 'until' (a time limit). It should be 'so that they are able to' or 'to be able to'. The web keys disagree ((a) vs (b)); DP keeps (b).
Answer: (b).
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose (d).

__Since he was going to live in South Korea for some time,__ (a) __he thought he should__ (b) __learn something about their culture.__ (c)

Concept: 'Since' can introduce a reason that the listener already knows, and 'their culture' refers to the people of Korea.
Step 1: All three parts are acceptable. The web keys disagree ((a) vs (d)); DP keeps (d).
Answer: (d) No error.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose (d).

Concept: Subject-verb agreement.
Step 1: The subject 'success' is singular, so 'is largely due to'.
Answer: (b).
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.theme: Stative verb not used in continuous

__I am owning__ (a) __two houses__ (b) __in Bengaluru.__ (c)

questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:

__A boy was injured__ (a) __in the accident and was taken__ (b) __onto hospital.__ (c)

questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:

__Mr. Malhotra is a historian__ (a) __who's books__ (b) __have won international acclaim.__ (c)

questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

__I hate it__ (a) __when I break__ (b) __in hives.__ (c)

questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

__Either Vikas__ (a) __or his friends__ (b) __is going to cook dinner.__ (c)

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.question:

Psychological problems among the youth can be attributed to the __pernicious__ influence of the Internet.

questions.question:

questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word.

The actor narrated the story in a __resonant__ voice.

Concept: Synonym.

Answer: (c) deep.
questions.source: CDS II 2024 English set A (set code RAKU-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word.

They were fed-up with his __doltish__ behaviour.

questions.theme: Joining sentences with the right connector
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the option that most appropriately combines both sentences into one sentence.

He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him. He did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution.
questions.opt_a: He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him as because he did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution.
questions.opt_b: He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him due to he did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution.
questions.opt_c: He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him since he did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution.
questions.opt_d: He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him whenever he did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Choose the connector that matches the relationship between the two sentences.
Step 1: The second sentence gives the reason, so 'since' is right. 'as because' and 'due to he' are ungrammatical, and 'whenever' gives a wrong sense.
Answer: (c) He was adamant about refusing the honour bestowed upon him since he did not trust the credentials of the organisation that intended to recognise his contribution..
